title: How to Adapt to Living Abroad: Tips That Actually Work
summary: Struggling to settle in a new country? Learn how to adapt to living abroad with practical, honest tips that help you feel at home faster.
body_markdown:
[Living Abroad](https://blog.transfez.com/en/living-abroad/)


You packed your bags, boarded the flight, and landed in a brand-new country full of excitement. Then, about two weeks in, reality hits. The food is different, the language trips you up, and you miss your mom’s cooking more than you ever thought possible. Sound familiar? You are definitely not alone.[Living abroad](https://blog.transfez.com/en/living-abroad-tips/) is one of the most rewarding things a person can do, but the adjustment period can feel genuinely tough.


The good news? Adapting to life in a new country is a skill, and like any skill, you can get better at it with the right approach. This guide breaks down how to adapt to living abroad in a way that is honest, practical, and actually useful, whether you just arrived or have been struggling to settle in for months.

##


**Why Adapting Abroad Feels So Hard at First**


Before we jump into solutions, it helps to understand what is actually happening when you feel out of place in a new country. This experience even has a name: *culture shock* . It is not just missing home food or struggling with the language. It is a deeper psychological adjustment to an entirely new set of social rules, expectations, and rhythms of daily life.


###


**1. The Four Stages of Culture Shock**


Most people go through a predictable pattern when they move abroad. Knowing where you are in the cycle can make the hard moments feel far less scary.


- **Honeymoon stage:** Everything feels exciting and fresh. You are a tourist in your own new life.
- **Frustration stage:** The novelty wears off. Small daily things start to irritate you. This is where most people struggle.
- **Adjustment stage:** You start to find your rhythm. Things that confused you begin to make sense.
- **Acceptance stage:** You feel genuinely comfortable. You might even prefer some things about your new country over home.


Everyone moves through these stages at a different pace. Some people breeze through frustration in a month. Others sit in it for six months or more. Both are completely normal.


###


**2. The Hidden Stress of Starting Over**


When you move abroad, you lose your entire social infrastructure overnight. Your friend group, your favourite spots, your daily routines, your sense of competence in navigating everyday life, all of it resets to zero. That is genuinely exhausting, even if the move was your choice and you are happy about it. Give yourself permission to acknowledge that it is hard without feeling like you made a mistake.


##


**Practical Steps to Adapt Faster**


Okay, enough theory. Here is what actually helps when you are trying to figure out how to adapt to living abroad and want to feel settled sooner rather than later.


###


**1. Build a Routine as Fast as Possible**


Routine is the antidote to chaos. When everything around you is unfamiliar, a predictable daily structure gives your brain something solid to hold onto. Pick a regular morning routine, a go-to grocery store, a weekly activity you commit to. These anchors matter more than you think.


###


**2. Learn at Least the Basics of the Local Language**


You do not need to be fluent. But being able to greet people, order food, ask for directions, and apologise in the local language changes everything. Locals respond differently when they see you making the effort. It also builds your confidence in a tangible way. Download a language app, take a beginner class, or just practise with neighbours.


###


**3. Join Something, Anything**


Isolation is the enemy of adaptation. Join a sports club, a language exchange group, a cooking class, a volunteer programme, a community of fellow Indonesians abroad. The social connection does not have to be deep right away. Just showing up consistently somewhere builds familiarity, and familiarity builds belonging. This is one of the most underrated tips for[Indonesians living abroad](https://blog.transfez.com/en/indonesian-diaspora-living-abroad-complete-guide/) who want to settle in faster.


###


**4. Explore Your Neighbourhood Like a Local**


Resist the urge to stay indoors or only visit tourist spots. Walk around your neighbourhood without a destination. Find the corner bakery. Learn which park locals actually use. Discover the cheap lunch spot that has no English menu but always has a queue. These small discoveries make a place feel like *yours* .


###


**5. Stay Connected Back Home, But Not Too Much**


Keeping in touch with family and friends back in Indonesia is important for your mental health. But there is a balance. If every spare moment is spent video calling home or scrolling through Indonesian news, you create a mental barrier to actually engaging with where you are now. Schedule your calls, enjoy them fully, then put your phone down and step outside.


###


**6. Be Curious Instead of Judgmental**


When something local confuses or frustrates you, try leading with curiosity rather than criticism. Ask why things work a certain way. Research the cultural background. You will often find that what seemed bizarre actually makes complete sense in context. This mindset shift is one of the biggest differences between people who thrive abroad and people who struggle.


###


**7. Take Care of Your Physical Health**


Sleep, exercise, and eating well are not luxuries during an adjustment period. They are necessities. When your body is run down, every emotional challenge feels three times harder. Prioritise the basics, even when your schedule feels chaotic from all the settling-in tasks.


##


**Managing Homesickness Without Letting It Hold You Back**


Homesickness is real and it is not a sign of weakness. Even people who absolutely love their new country get hit by it, usually at unexpected moments like a public holiday or hearing a familiar song. The key is learning to hold space for that feeling without letting it derail you.


###


**1. Create Small Pieces of Home in Your New Space**


Cook an Indonesian meal once a week. Display a photo that makes you smile. Keep a comfort item from home on your desk. These small gestures remind your brain that your identity and your roots travel with you, regardless of your address.


###


**2. Find Your Community**


Whether it is an Indonesian student association, an expat meetup, or an online group, finding people who understand your background matters. You can vent about the things that are hard without having to explain the full cultural context. This kind of community is invaluable, especially in the early months. If you are a student, you might find inspiration in[real stories from people who have studied abroad](https://blog.transfez.com/en/what-it-feels-like-to-study-abroad/) and navigated exactly this.


###


**3. Reframe the Hard Days**


On a difficult day, it helps to remind yourself why you made this move. Write it down if you need to. Reconnecting with your original motivation, whether that is career growth, education, adventure, or a fresh start, can give a hard week a lot more meaning.


##


**Practical Life Admin That Speeds Up Adaptation**


A lot of the friction of living abroad comes from unresolved logistics. The faster you sort out the practical side of life, the faster your brain can relax and start actually enjoying where you are.


- Get a local bank account set up as soon as you can.
- Register with local government services if your country of residence requires it.
- Find a reliable doctor or healthcare provider before you actually need one.
- Sort out a reliable way to send money home to Indonesia. Using a dedicated international remittance service like **Transfez** can make this part of life much smoother, so it is one less thing on your mind.
- Set up your local transport options, whether that is a transit card, a bike, or learning the bus routes.


Every item you tick off that list removes a low-level stress from your daily life. And less background stress means more mental energy for the fun parts of living in a new country.

Be patient with yourself, stay curious, and trust that the discomfort you feel right now is part of a process that genuinely leads somewhere great.
